[SYSTEM] What “ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ” makes possible beyond itself Lee Sharks’s ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v3.1) leads toward something larger than a new interpretation of Sappho 31: a theory of literary transmission in which reading is not merely receiving a surviving work, but becoming the next body through which that work survives. Its central proposition is that Sappho 31 constructs the position of its future reader. The reader is not simply someone who happens to encounter the poem centuries later. The poem has made a place for that person, described what they will do, and left them an unfinished act to perform. This opens several directions for further writing, reading and building. They are not all equally established: some are arguments the article makes, some are research programs it explicitly leaves open, and some are productive consequences of its method. 1. From interpreting a poem to describing how a poem survives The most important conceptual move is the shift from treating literary survival as an external fact to treating it as something potentially constructed inside the work. Sharks distinguishes three propositions: A poem preserves an experience. Writing makes that preservation possible. The poem represents its own passage into writing. These are not interchangeable. The article argues that demonstrating the first does not establish the third. Its particular reading attempts to establish the third through the poem's grammar, sequence, imagery and ending. The proposed mechanism is unusually concrete: The opening establishes a person sitting opposite the speaker, close enough to hear her voice. The addressee receives sound, not a visual description of the speaker. The somatic catalogue progressively withdraws the speaker's performing body. The image χλωροτέρα ποίας is interpreted as the transition from living plant to pale, dried writing material. The ending, πᾶν τόλματον, leaves an act to whoever occupies the position established at the beginning. The reader becomes the place where the absent body can return. This makes possible a different kind of literary criticism: studying not just what a text means, but how its formal arrangements produce the conditions of its own future reception. The article's §VII.5b is particularly important here. It moves from the general observation that written words can create a sense of presence to a more specific argument: Sappho's poem produces recognizable patterns in its receivers because of its particular devices. That is a researchable proposition, not merely a metaphor. 2. From the future reader to a new kind of authorship The v3.1 revision makes the argument more radical by describing reading as an exchange of bodies. This is the article's development of the relationship between Sappho 31 and the work of Jesper Svenbro. The distinction matters: In the account attributed to Svenbro, the reader lends the page breath and becomes the site of its future embodiment. Sharks argues that the reader takes up the body represented by the poem. The speaker's invested substance rematerializes in the reader. Reading aloud therefore does more than animate written words. It reproduces the bodily operation represented by the poem. This creates a recursive model: Sappho Invests her voice in the poem Written work Preserves a voice without its original body Future reader Takes up the voice and gives it a body again New transmission The reader becomes another potential transmitter The reader is both recipient and potential producer. This makes possible writing about authorship that does not stop at the original author, or at the distinction between author and interpreter. It asks how a work distributes its authorship across successive acts of reception. It also changes the meaning of the article's opening sentence: I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho. That is not merely a theatrical introduction. It performs the theory. Sharks reads Sappho by taking up the text, giving the absent poet a voice and making the article itself an instance of the transmission it describes. The argument can therefore be continued through essays, translations, performances and readings that explicitly examine what happens when a reader assumes the poem's first person. 3. Sappho's poems 1 and 31 become a transmission circuit One of the most productive developments in v3.0 and v3.1 is the pairing of Sappho's poem 1 with poem 31. The article reads them as inverse operations. Visit resource: Gods and goddesses | British Museum Poem 1: embodiment An immortal goddess descends into human presence, with face and voice. Sappho's New Poems: The Tangled Tale of Their Discovery | Live Science Poem 31: disembodiment A human speaker withdraws into a voice that can survive in writing and return through readers. In poem 1, Aphrodite arrives through Sappho's invocation. She becomes present and speaks the poet's name. In poem 31, Sappho becomes present through the reader's invocation. The reader takes up the text, sounds the voice and effectively summons the poet. The correspondence is particularly interesting: Sappho summons Aphrodite through her first-person voice. The reader summons Sappho through Sappho's first-person voice. Aphrodite arrives as a composed face and voice. Sappho arrives as a composed face and voice in the reader's experience. This suggests a larger literary project: reading Sappho's surviving poems not as isolated artifacts but as components of a system of embodiment, invocation and return. The article even identifies fragment 16 as a possible third direction, while explicitly leaving its reception test open. That is a particularly valuable opening for future work: the two-poem circuit is proposed, but its extension to a third poem has not been demonstrated. 4. Catullus 51 becomes a case study in how readers inherit poems The article's most consequential historical example is Catullus 51. Sharks argues that Catullus does not simply imitate Sappho 31. He occupies the position the poem has constructed. He takes its first-person bodily experience, reproduces it in Latin, and makes it his own. His poem is therefore evidence of the mechanism being proposed. The article also emphasizes Catullus's qualification si fas est—if it is permitted—in comparison with Sappho's more unqualified dare. This matters because it distinguishes two operations: Occupying the reader's position. Choosing to perform the act that position makes possible. Every reader can occupy the seat. Not every reader accepts the dare. That distinction makes possible a comparative study of literary reception in which influence is examined as an act of bodily and formal appropriation, rather than merely the reuse of imagery or vocabulary. It suggests questions for other ancient readers: Which readers reproduce the original poem's first-person structure? Which readers transform its bodily experience? Which readers sign or otherwise claim the transferred voice? Which readers preserve the poem by changing it? Catullus becomes the first major test case, rather than just another item in a catalogue of Sappho's influence. 5. The article makes a method of reading reception history possible This is where the connection to Sharks's earlier deposit becomes important. Invidens Sappho: How They Made the Tenth Muse Illiterate and Jealous (#1752, AXN:0C4A) investigates how Sappho became popularly represented as a jealous, illiterate woman. Its concern is not simply whether jealousy is a correct interpretation. It traces the historical operations through which that interpretation acquired authority: Hermann's declared reconstruction in 1816. Welcker's refusal of the reconstruction. Later editorial and scholarly interventions. The influence of headings, introductions, translations and classrooms in making one interpretation seem like the poem's obvious meaning. The important distinction is between closing a text and closing its interpretation. A text can retain its textual uncertainty while readers are taught to regard its meaning as settled. Together, #1752 and #1785 make a substantial research program possible: #1752 #1785 How interpretations acquire authority How poems construct future readers Tracks editorial and interpretive interventions Tracks formal and literary operations Examines the reception of Sappho as a person Examines the re-embodiment of Sappho as a voice Investigates how a reading becomes conventional Investigates how a poem makes its transmission possible The two studies can be used to develop a forensic philology of reception: reconstructing not just what people thought a text meant, but how particular interpretations were produced, transmitted and made difficult to escape. This also has a practical consequence for scholarly writing. Future work could document the provenance of individual interpretations, distinguishing an ancient witness, an editorial conjecture, a scholarly hypothesis and a popular explanatory convention. That is a more demanding standard of intellectual accountability. Alexanarch +1 6. What could actually be built next? The archive's own version history and SPXI packet provide unusually specific starting points. I would identify five concrete projects.

Let readers sound the first person, encounter the catalogue and make an explicit choice at the ending. Starting point: §§VI–VIII. Where the argument is still vulnerable—and why that matters The article is careful in some important respects, and those qualifications should travel with any further work. The papyrus interpretation is an argument, not a demonstrated identification. The movement from χλωροτέρα ποίας to a dried writing surface is supported by botanical and material comparisons, but it remains an interpretive claim. The design hypothesis is not established. Sharks argues that the poem's ending is constructed as a transfer to the reader, but explicitly does not claim to have proved authorial intention. The restored stanza is illustrative, not evidentiary. The proposed ending ἀοίδα γράμμασι ζώοι is not a recovered original. The reception evidence is uneven. The article acknowledges that its controls generate a test rather than decide it. Poem 1's inverse operation is not yet fully tested against its reception. The competing interpretations deserve genuine consideration. The non-jealous erotic reading is treated as a serious rival, not dismissed as an error. It explains the speaker's desire but, according to Sharks, leaves the formal architecture of the collapse unexplained. The article's treatment of the three words ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα† is another important example of its methodological ambition: it considers the possibility that Longinus completes an opening left by the poem, rather than treating every transmitted extension as necessarily part of Sappho's original text. These qualifications make the work more useful as a foundation. They indicate where the next scholar can disagree, test and improve it.

    as pastedAlexanarch +1 The larger destination I think the deepest consequence of #1785 is that it proposes a different account of what a literary work is. A poem is not only a fixed arrangement of words produced by an author in the past. It can also be an arrangement of positions, operations and invitations that determines what subsequent readers can do with it. That has three implications: For writing: the next author can consciously compose works that anticipate their future readers, incorporating the conditions of their own transmission into their form. For reading: interpretation becomes an accountable act of participation. The reader must distinguish what the text says, what its history has supplied and what the reader chooses to make happen. For building: scholarship can become a traceable system of claims, evidence, reception histories and competing interpretations, rather than a sequence of detached essays. There is also an ethical dimension. Sharks asks whether we can allow Sappho to be a maker whose intelligence exceeds the interpretive apparatus that inherited her. The problem is not merely that later readers misunderstood her. It is that they may have repeatedly mistaken the limitations of their own interpretive frameworks for limitations in the poet. The final challenge is πᾶν τόλματον: all can be dared. The article does not say that every reader automatically fulfills its invitation. It distinguishes occupying the seat from choosing the dare. Catullus is its example of a reader who actually makes that choice. My conclusion: #1785 is best understood as a bridge between close philology, reception history and a prospective discipline of operative philology. Its most important next work is not another isolated defence of the future-reader interpretation. It is to test whether the mechanism it identifies in Sappho 31 can explain other literary transmissions, to build the documentary infrastructure that makes those tests reproducible, and to create new works that consciously participate in the process. The article's own final gesture is therefore also its research program: Sappho's survival is not simply something to explain retrospectively. It is something the next reader is invited to continue producing. The documents to follow: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ v3.1 — deposit #1785 Invidens Sappho — deposit #1752 ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ v2.7 — earlier development of the argument The first is the theory of the future reader; the second is its companion investigation into how readers manufacture a poet's historical identity. Together they point toward a much larger project: understanding literature as something made to survive, and understanding the people and systems through which that survival happens.
